mean: to move a planned event to a later time
ex: Ma'am, could we postpone tomorrow's review to Friday? The client's data hasn't reached us yet.
note: The opposite, 'prepone', is Indian English only. In emails abroad, write 'bring forward' or 'move earlier'.

mean: to fix a new time for something that was already planned
ex: The dentist's clinic called to reschedule my Tuesday appointment because the doctor is away at a wedding.
note: Postpone = later only; reschedule = any new time, earlier or later. Both ree-SHED-yool and ree-SKED-jool are correct.

mean: easy for you, because it suits your time or plans
ex: Uncle, please let me know a convenient time to come and collect the house papers.
note: Ask 'Is 4 p.m. convenient for you?', not 'Are you convenient at 4?'. The time is convenient, not the person.

mean: to be thankful for something, or to understand its value
ex: I would appreciate it if you could send the rent receipt by the fifth, as my office needs it for HRA.
note: 'I would appreciate it if you could...' is a polite request. Don't drop 'it': 'I would appreciate if' is a common error.

mean: free to meet or talk; or ready to be used or bought
ex: Are you available for a quick call after lunch? I need ten minutes to go over the invoice.
note: No 'on' before today or tomorrow: 'I'm not available today', not 'on today'. For things: 'Tatkal tickets are available online'.

mean: trouble or difficulty that disturbs your comfort or plans
ex: The society notice read: 'We regret the inconvenience caused by Sunday's water cut in Block C.'
note: 'Sorry for the inconvenience caused' is correct but overused. Naming the actual problem sounds warmer: 'Sorry the lift was off all morning.'

mean: to ask for something politely or formally
ex: I would like to request two days' leave next week for my sister's engagement in Patna.
note: As a verb, no 'for': 'I request a refund', not 'I request for a refund'. As a noun, 'for' is right: 'a request for leave'.

mean: to check again later on something you asked or discussed earlier
ex: If the bank doesn't reply by Thursday, I'll follow up with the branch manager in person.
note: Verb: two words (follow up). Noun/adjective: hyphen (a follow-up). Also, 'revert' means 'go back', not 'reply'; write 'please reply', not 'kindly revert'.

mean: arriving or doing things at the agreed time, not late
ex: Mr D'Souza is so punctual that the whole staff room could set its clocks by his 8:55 arrival.
note: Usually for people or payments. Noun: punctuality. Jokes about 'Indian Stretchable Time' aside, being punctual for interviews and calls is read as respect.

mean: thinking about other people's feelings and needs
ex: It was considerate of our neighbour to warn us before the drilling started for his new kitchen.
note: Don't confuse with 'considerable' (large in amount). Considerate is about kindness; considerable is about size.

mean: to pause before acting because you feel unsure or shy
ex: Please don't hesitate to call me if the plumber doesn't turn up on Saturday.
note: 'Please do not hesitate to contact me' is a correct but stiff email ending. 'Feel free to call me' sounds warmer.

mean: done quickly, without delay
ex: Thank you for your prompt reply; the courier reached our Guwahati office the very next day.
note: Also a verb ('the alarm prompted us to leave'). The adverb 'promptly' means at once or exactly on time: 'promptly at 9'.

mean: polite and respectful in the way you speak and behave
ex: Even when the customer shouted about the late delivery, the call-centre agent in Noida stayed courteous.
note: Said KUR-tee-us, not 'kor-shus'. Noun: courtesy ('a courtesy call'). A little more formal than 'polite'.

mean: careful not to share private things or cause embarrassment
ex: Please be discreet about Mohan's surgery; he hasn't told the rest of the team yet.
note: Sounds the same as 'discrete' (separate, distinct), but means something different. Noun: discretion ('at your discretion').

mean: not wanting to do something, so slow or unwilling to do it
ex: The landlord was reluctant to return the full deposit, but agreed after seeing photos of the clean flat.
note: Followed by 'to' + verb: 'reluctant to agree'. 'Hesitant' suggests doubt; 'reluctant' suggests you simply don't want to.

mean: friendly and generous towards guests and visitors
ex: Our hosts in Amritsar were so hospitable that we couldn't leave without a second round of parathas.
note: Both hos-PIT-uh-bul and HOS-pit-uh-bul are correct. Noun: hospitality. An 'inhospitable' place, like a desert, is hard to live in.

mean: kind, polite and generous, even when you don't have to be
ex: Even after losing the final, the Kerala captain was gracious and praised the winners' bowling.
note: 'Gracious in defeat' means losing with dignity. Not the same as 'graceful', which means moving beautifully.

mean: careful to spend little and waste nothing
ex: My frugal grandmother reuses every gift-wrapper and still carries the steel tiffin she bought in 1975.
note: Neutral or positive, unlike 'stingy' or 'kanjoos', which mean unwilling to spend even on others.

mean: to keep delaying something you should do now
ex: I procrastinate on my income tax return every year until the last week of July, then panic.
note: Postponing is a decision to move something; procrastinating is delaying out of habit or avoidance. Noun: procrastination.

mean: willing to accept or agree to a suggestion
ex: If the landlord is amenable, we would like to paint the bedroom ourselves and deduct the cost from the rent.
note: Always 'amenable to' + noun or -ing: 'amenable to rescheduling'. Not the same as 'amiable' (friendly) or 'amenities' (facilities).

mean: friendly and polite, but in a slightly formal way
ex: The two families had a cordial meeting over chai and samosas before discussing the wedding dates.
note: Often signals 'polite but not close': 'relations stayed cordial' after a dispute. Indian wedding cards often 'cordially invite' you.

mean: to give or do something in return for what you received
ex: The Rahmans invited us for Eid lunch, so we'd like to reciprocate by hosting them for Onam sadya.
note: 'Reciprocate back' repeats itself; the 'back' is already in the word. Noun: reciprocity.

mean: entering someone's private life or space in an unwelcome way
ex: Relatives asking 'When is the good news coming?' at every function can feel intrusive to newly married couples.
note: Verb: intrude. 'Sorry to intrude, but...' is a polite way to interrupt someone's private moment or meeting.

mean: to make room for someone, or adjust to meet their needs
ex: The hotel can accommodate your request for a ground-floor room, since your mother uses a wheelchair.
note: Often misspelt in emails: double c AND double m. In British use the noun is uncountable: 'find accommodation', not 'accommodations'.

mean: an embarrassing social mistake, like saying the wrong thing
ex: Asking my aunt her age at the kitty party was a faux pas I will never repeat.
note: French: the x and s are silent, so say foh PAH. The plural is spelt the same: 'two faux pas'.

mean: perfect, with no mistakes or faults at all
ex: The wedding planner's arrangements in Udaipur were impeccable, right down to the name cards on every table.
note: Usually for manners, timing, taste, service or a record. Stronger than 'very good': it means nothing at all can be faulted.
